title: Repilot

jokes.text: Jeff's low-budget lawyer TV commercial opens with a dramatic villain monologue ('I am the system. I consume humanity. There is no escape.') before Jeff heroically interjects
jokes.setup: Ominous villainous voice-over sets up an action-movie tone
jokes.punchline: 'Objection! Jeff Winger, hero-at-law. Best lawyer you ever saw.' — a cheesy, rhyming local TV ad parody that undercuts the epic opening
jokes.explanation: The cold open parody of cheap local lawyer commercials is perfectly calibrated for Jeff's character — a once-arrogant hotshot reduced to bad jingles. The rhyming couplet 'hero-at-law / best lawyer you ever saw' is specifically embarrassing in a way that suits his arc. Strong character integration and structural discipline.

dialogue.speaker: Voiceover
dialogue.line: I am the system.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You can't fight me. I am the system.

dialogue.speaker: Voiceover
dialogue.line: But one man dared to try...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Jeff Winger: Hero at Law. Call now and we'll validate your parking!

jokes.text: 'Maybe you should've spent less money on special effects.' / 'Yeah. Thanks a lot, Francis Ford Repo Man.'
jokes.setup: Jeff's commercial has expensive-looking production value but is clearly low-budget and ineffective
jokes.punchline: The 'Francis Ford Repo Man' insult — a portmanteau of Francis Ford Coppola and a repo man — mocking the pretentious production ambition of a failed lawyer ad
jokes.explanation: 'Francis Ford Repo Man' is a sharp, economical insult — it condenses pretension + failure into three words. The structure is tight: Alan's straight-line sets up Jeff's self-deprecating snark. Good economy, clever reference construction.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Yeah, Jeff, you really went overboard with the green screen budget on this one.

jokes.text: On-screen text reading 'Jeff Winger, loser-at-law. Rented office in a mini mall.'
jokes.setup: The commercial opened with 'Jeff Winger, hero-at-law'
jokes.punchline: The revised chyron 'loser-at-law / rented office in a mini mall' — the same rhyme scheme now brutally deflating his status
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback — reuses the exact rhyme scheme from the opening but inverts it completely. 'Mini mall' as the punchline word is specifically humiliating, and the economy is exceptional. This is the kind of tight construction Community is known for.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, so I'm not a good enough director for you? Well at least I'm not a Francis Ford Repo Man.

jokes.text: 'Relax, Tango. I come in peace.' — Jeff's nickname for Alan suggests their history is a tense dance
jokes.setup: Jeff walks into what is clearly hostile territory to meet his former colleague
jokes.punchline: 'Relax, Tango' — a casual, slightly absurd nickname that implies Jeff still thinks he has the social upper hand despite being a mini-mall lawyer
jokes.explanation: Functional character-comedy beat. Jeff's breezy confidence in a humiliating situation is consistent and mildly amusing, but 'Tango' as a nickname doesn't land with particular force. Mid-tier joke.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Loser at Law. Jeff Winger: couldn't pass the bar exam. Couldn't keep a steady job. Couldn't maintain a healthy relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm Jeff Winger, and I'm a loser.

jokes.text: 'A human could say that without salivating.' — Jeff responds to Alan's excited pitch about the bridge collapse case
jokes.setup: Alan describes the bridge collapse as a 'juicy new client' and a 'bone to throw'
jokes.punchline: Jeff notes that a human could describe a legal opportunity without drooling — implying Alan is a predatory non-human
jokes.explanation: Very economical burn. 'A human could say that without salivating' works on multiple levels — it's an insult, a character sketch of Alan, and an echo of Jeff's own former predatory nature. The word 'salivating' does a lot of heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Hey there, tango. What's up?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Did you just call me 'tango'?

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's what I call my buddies. Also, I've been using it to contact aliens. They seem really into it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... not how any of this works.

jokes.text: 'From what? His own pencil?' — Jeff's response to Alan saying the bridge engineer wants to seek damages
jokes.setup: Alan says the bridge engineer who designed a collapsed bridge wants to seek damages
jokes.punchline: Jeff's instant retort — 'From what? His own pencil?' — points out the absurdity of the engineer being a victim when he designed the faulty bridge
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — three words nail the absurdity perfectly. 'His own pencil' is a sharp, specific image that captures the engineer's culpability with zero waste. This is Jeff's wit at its best: fast, specific, and devastating. Near-8 caliber.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: This bridge collapse case is the most exciting thing that's happened to me in years!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... that's really concerning, Alan. The way you're talking about structural failure and potential loss of life — it's like watching a predator get excited about wounded prey.

jokes.text: 'Weird choice, by the way, bachelor's degree on the wall.' — Jeff notices a framed degree in Alan's office
jokes.setup: Alan is a successful lawyer; Jeff notices he has a framed bachelor's degree displayed
jokes.punchline: Calling it a 'weird choice' — only someone insecure would display a bachelor's degree; graduate degrees and law degrees are display-worthy, but a BA signals you have nothing better
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational beat. Jeff spots a social tell and uses it to subtly assert dominance even from a position of weakness. Fits his character well. Loses points because the joke requires audience inference, slightly diluting the impact.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so the engineer is gonna sue himself? That's like... suing yourself. Which is just therapy.

jokes.text: 'Jeff, I once saw you convince an arson victim that he liked his house better burnt.'
jokes.setup: Alan is trying to convince Jeff that Greendale 'ruined' him by making him care about people
jokes.punchline: The specific, absurd example of convincing an arson victim he preferred his house on fire — capturing Jeff's former sociopathic legal genius
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity is what elevates it — not just 'you were a good manipulator' but *this exact scenario*. 'He liked his house better burnt' is a genuinely funny image that also works as character backstory delivered as comedy. High quotability, strong character integration, dark-comic edge.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I'm going to sue Greendale for everything they've got. I need a lawyer. Jeff, you went to law school, right?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I did, yes.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Well, that was a mistake, but will you help me anyway?

jokes.text: 'And worst of all, it took your Winger moves.' / 'I still got my Winger moves.' / 'Prove it.'
jokes.setup: Alan lists what Greendale 'took' from Jeff — his money, his time, his edge
jokes.punchline: Culminating in 'your Winger moves' — a ridiculous self-brand — and Jeff's defensive, slightly pathetic insistence that he still has them
jokes.explanation: 'Winger moves' as a self-brand is funny in its grandiosity and vagueness. Jeff's reflexive defense of them when humiliated is consistent and amusing. Good character work, though the line doesn't have the snap of the best jokes here.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Jeff, your closing argument was so persuasive, you convinced a jury that a man didn't commit murder even though he was literally holding the knife.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, technically the knife was holding him.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: The knife was holding a dead body.

jokes.text: 'I might be broke, desperate, nearly homeless, but I still got one thing deep down inside that gives me power...' [beat] 'That was it. That was all I had.'
jokes.setup: Classic inspirational speech setup — Jeff begins a 'I still have X' motivational declaration
jokes.punchline: The pause reveals the speech itself was the thing — he had nothing. The admission of total emptiness delivered as a deflated non-punchline
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The structure is immaculate: the setup mimics every inspirational Jeff Winger speech template, the pause creates genuine suspense, then 'That was it. That was all I had.' collapses the entire heroic-speech genre. It's also genuinely sad in a way that makes it funnier and more resonant. Exceptional economy and character integration — only Jeff's specific story makes this land. Comparable to 8+ anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: You help me, or I'm gonna make you work the streets.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's right. I know people. You'll be out there in a tube top and hot pants by next Tuesday.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton announces Greendale is 'ranked America's number two community college by greendalecommunitycollege.com'
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton delivers a proud ranking announcement
jokes.punchline: The ranking source is Greendale's own website — they ranked themselves number two on their own site
jokes.explanation: Classic Community Greendale-incompetence joke. The self-citation for a self-ranking is a quick, clean institutional-satire gag. The fact that they ranked themselves *number two* (not even first) adds an extra layer of pathetic self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You want to know the secret source of my power? The thing that makes me so irresistible, so confident, so devastatingly effective?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's... that was it. That's all I had.

jokes.text: 'We'll be observing a moment of silence on the quad, followed by four years of silence to the press.'
jokes.setup: Dean addresses the bridge collapse tragedy with an apparently sincere moment-of-silence announcement
jokes.punchline: He casually adds 'followed by four years of silence to the press' — a cover-up delivered with the same bureaucratic warmth as the memorial
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. The rhythm of 'moment of silence... followed by four years of silence to the press' is pitch-perfect — the parallelism makes the cover-up feel like a natural institutional continuation of grief. Only Dean Pelton, in his oblivious bureaucratic mode, could deliver this. Dark, well-structured, highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I have some exciting news. Greendale has been ranked number one!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: According to our website.

jokes.text: 'Shut up, Leonard. I'm not here. I'm just a figment of your creeping dementia.'
jokes.setup: Leonard, the recurring elderly student, spots Jeff and presumably says 'I told you you'd be back'
jokes.punchline: Jeff denies his presence and pivots to a brutal age-joke: he's not real, just Leonard's dementia hallucinating him
jokes.explanation: 'Creeping dementia' is a surprisingly dark escalation from 'I'm not here' and it's very specific to Jeff's character — his dismissals are always cruelly creative. The line also does double duty as a callback to Jeff's denial about returning to Greendale. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Let us observe a moment of silence for those lost in the bridge tragedy.

jokes.text: Jeff calls the records clerk 'Rita' and she corrects him 'Rhonda' — he pivots immediately: 'I've always regretted not telling you how much you remind me of my aunt.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is attempting to charm the records clerk but gets her name wrong
jokes.punchline: Rather than apologizing, he seamlessly pivots to a fake-intimate compliment that has nothing to do with her name — demonstrating his manipulation instinct even when impaired
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff manipulation — the pivot from wrong-name to fake-intimate compliment is both revealing and funny. Shows his social reflexes are intact even when his life isn't. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: I predicted you'd come back.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, I predicted that by now you'd be in a home, but here you are, still remembering your own name. Miracles happen.

jokes.text: 'It's more disarming than it sounds. I have a very attractive aunt.'
jokes.setup: Jeff's 'you remind me of my aunt' line sounds more creepy than charming on its face
jokes.punchline: Jeff's aside to us (or to himself) explaining it works because his aunt is attractive — which makes it worse AND explains his obliviousness
jokes.explanation: The aside adds a second layer to the already-funny charm attempt — not only does he think it works, he has a weirdly specific rationale for why. 'Very attractive aunt' is a phrase that shouldn't be as funny as it is. Good economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your memory is so bad, you probably forgot you even have dementia.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Phhhhbbbttt!

jokes.text: 'After you and your friends left, it was closed for sentimental reasons.' [beat] 'And asbestos reasons, but it's clean as a whistle now.'
jokes.setup: Dean explains the study room was closed out of emotional respect for the departed group
jokes.punchline: The sentimental reason is immediately undercut by the mundane health hazard — 'asbestos reasons' — and then immediately dismissed with 'clean as a whistle'
jokes.explanation: Solid Dean Pelton beat — the structure of sentiment-then-health-crisis is a reliable Community formula but executed well here. The quick reassurance 'clean as a whistle' after casually mentioning asbestos is the right comedic rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, I have to say, you remind me of my aunt.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.line: Oh, that's sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, she's really hot.

jokes.text: Abed: 'It's a callback to when we met first season. Me calling years "seasons" is a callback to my dialogue...' Jeff: 'I know what makes you off-putting...'
jokes.setup: Abed appears in the study room and immediately begins explaining the meta-narrative significance of his own entrance
jokes.punchline: Jeff interrupts to say he knows what makes Abed off-putting — a beat that acknowledges and validates the audience's reaction to Abed's hyper-self-awareness
jokes.explanation: This is a meta-joke that works on three levels simultaneously: Abed calling years 'seasons' is a real Community joke; him explaining it as a callback is itself a callback joke; Jeff's reaction ('I know what makes you off-putting') is the audience's voice. The episode is literally called 'Repilot' and Abed is narrating the repilot mechanics. Only Abed could deliver this, only Community would write it, and Jeff's interruption is the perfect valve. Near-exceptional.

jokes.text: Jeff says he figured everyone had careers to get started. The group responds with increasingly hollow affirmations: 'Yeah, working hard.' / 'Yes.' / 'Yeah. So many things.' / 'Yeah. Sandwiches... Us, always doing stuff.'
jokes.setup: Jeff assumes his friends are thriving in their post-Greendale lives
jokes.punchline: The cascading non-answers — especially 'Sandwiches... Us, always doing stuff' — reveal they have nothing going on, with each response worse than the last
jokes.explanation: The escalating hollow affirmations work as a group comedic beat. 'Sandwiches... Us, always doing stuff' is specifically funny because of how hard Shirley (presumably) is reaching. Good structural discipline in the escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Rhonda, we go way back. Remember when we used to hang out?

dialogue.speaker: Rhonda
dialogue.line: My name is Rhonda.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Right, right. So Brenda, about that favor I need...

jokes.text: Abed: 'We can repilot. This could be like Scrubs season nine, a revamp, a do-over. Jeff could come back as a teacher.'
jokes.setup: The group is emotionally reuniting in the study room
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately frames their real lives in terms of a TV show's season structure, specifically citing Scrubs season 9 as a template for a 'revamp'
jokes.explanation: The 'Scrubs season 9' reference is doing real work here — it's a specific, slightly niche reference about a real show that rebooted with a new cast, applied directly to Community's own situation as a show returning for a new season. Only Abed uses TV seasons as life frameworks, and the episode is literally titled 'Repilot.' Exceptional character integration and meta-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Jeff's return represents a profound moment of redemption and—actually, I'm just pitching this. Did it land? Should I try a different angle?

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I'm not gonna be a teacher, Abed.' [immediately cuts to Jeff being recruited as a teacher]
jokes.setup: Jeff firmly refuses the idea of becoming a teacher
jokes.punchline: Implicit in the episode structure — this denial precedes him becoming a teacher, which the audience knows from show marketing/context
jokes.explanation: Functional ironic setup that the episode will pay off. The denial is funny in context because Abed's framing is so specific and correct. Gets a rewatch bonus because on second viewing the dramatic irony is more pronounced.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm establishing the Greendale Human-Centipede Immersion Committee.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's just a working title, right?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: It is now.

jokes.text: Abed explains 'Repiloting can be intense. New people show up, regulars shift roles or even fall away. In Scrubs, Zach was only in the first six episodes.' Troy: 'That son of a bitch.' Britta: 'After everything Scrubs did for him?'
jokes.setup: Abed continues his Scrubs-season-9 framework for their situation
jokes.punchline: Troy and Britta express genuine betrayal-level outrage at Zach Braff's limited involvement in Scrubs season 9 — treating a TV production decision as a personal moral failing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Troy and Britta's instant, righteous fury at Zach Braff — 'That son of a bitch' / 'After everything Scrubs did for him?' — is perfect absurdist character comedy. The joke works because they treat fictional TV loyalty as a genuine moral framework. The escalation from Abed's analytical observation to Troy's visceral outrage to Britta's principled solidarity is structurally impeccable. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The study room is closed for sentimental reasons. Also, there's asbestos, but that's not really the main issue here.

jokes.text: Jeff gives an excuse to leave the room: 'I gotta go to the bathroom.' Abed: 'Give him space. Repiloting can be intense.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is emotionally overwhelmed by the reunion and the manipulation he's about to commit
jokes.punchline: Abed reframes Jeff's bathroom excuse as a narrative beat — 'repiloting can be intense' — continuing to treat their lives as a TV show
jokes.explanation: Functional extension of the Scrubs/repilot running gag. Abed's straight-faced analysis of a bathroom break as a narrative beat is amusing but slightly repetitive at this point in the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Remember when we first met? You were eating a sandwich and I told you that you were doing it wrong.

jokes.text: Jeff discovers an empty box labeled 'Humphries' on the Dean's desk. Dean explains he shredded the records to protect the school.
jokes.setup: Jeff told Alan that Greendale 'wouldn't shred evidence' because 'it's a good place for good people'
jokes.punchline: The Dean did exactly that — the labeled empty box is a visual punchline to Jeff's naive faith in the institution
jokes.explanation: Solid structural callback with a visual gag component — the empty box still labeled 'Humphries' is a perfect ironic image. The rewatch bonus is high because it retroactively reframes Jeff's earlier defense of Greendale.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm aware that I'm aware that I'm aware that I'm doing a callback to when I was aware that I was aware that I was doing a meta-commentary. Which is itself a meta-commentary on my meta-commentary about meta-commentary. And now I'm doing a meta-commentary on the meta-commentary about the meta-commentary about meta-commentary, which means I'm aware of being aware of being aware of being aware, and I can feel it spiraling, which is actually just another layer of meta-awareness that I'm now commenting on.

jokes.text: Dean: 'Okay. So sue me.' [immediately realizes what he said, in the middle of a lawsuit episode]
jokes.setup: The Dean is being defensive about shredding evidence in a case about suing Greendale
jokes.punchline: 'Okay. So sue me.' — an idiomatic expression that is literally accurate as a legal threat
jokes.explanation: Functional wordplay joke — the idiom becomes literal in context. It's a quick, competent gag but not especially inventive. The show doesn't dwell on it, which is correct.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know, the thing about meta-commentary is that it's simultaneously a deconstruction of narrative tropes while also being complicit in perpetuating those very tropes through its own self-aware acknowledgment of—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're doing it again.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'And that would be bad because...?' / Dean: 'Because then I wouldn't have a job. And, you know, Greendale is a good place for good people.'
jokes.setup: Jeff challenges the Dean's assumption that Greendale closing would be bad
jokes.punchline: The Dean's first honest answer is self-interest ('I wouldn't have a job'), then he tacks on the institutional platitude as an afterthought
jokes.explanation: Good beat. The Dean's honesty-then-spin is a small but precise character moment — he accidentally tells the truth before remembering his talking points. The callback to 'good place for good people' as a hollow slogan earns another small laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you guys!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know, right? This is amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I have missed you so much!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We need to do this every week!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Every day!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Every hour!

jokes.text: Alan arrives at the records room: 'Wing Blade. Shock me by impressing me.'
jokes.setup: Alan expects Jeff to have retrieved the files
jokes.punchline: 'Wing Blade' as a Jeff nickname (riffing on 'Winger') plus 'Shock me by impressing me' — a casually contemptuous challenge
jokes.explanation: Decent line. 'Wing Blade' is a reasonable villain nickname for Alan to use. 'Shock me by impressing me' is a good put-down rhythm. Mid-tier competent writing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So, we've all made it big in our respective fields, right?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm a... I'm doing really well with my...

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, definitely successful, very successful at my...

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've been working on some projects that are—

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: The business is really—

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: My company has been—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: ...guys?

jokes.text: 'My wife left, my girlfriend dumped me. And they're sisters, whole family's pissed.'
jokes.setup: Alan says the case was all he had and his life is falling apart
jokes.punchline: The escalation: not just relationship failures, but wife AND girlfriend — who are sisters — delivered as a matter-of-fact detail
jokes.explanation: Good dark escalation. The reveal that his wife and girlfriend are sisters is a classic escalating-revelation structure. 'Whole family's pissed' as the third beat is good economy. The joke characterizes Alan as both villainous and pathetic, which serves the narrative.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We should all drink the Kool-Aid together.

jokes.text: 'Season nine of Scrubs.' / 'And that's the Winger Guarantee.'
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals his plan to flip his friends into plaintiffs against Greendale
jokes.punchline: Abed summarizes it as 'Season nine of Scrubs' (the repilot strategy) while Jeff delivers his commercial catchphrase — both are ironic callbacks given Jeff is manipulating his friends
jokes.explanation: Double callback that works as a beat — 'Season nine of Scrubs' applied to Jeff's manipulation scheme recontextualizes the earlier meta-joke darkly, and 'Winger Guarantee' closing this scene echoes the failed commercial. Rewatch value is high.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're not really leaving. This is just a season finale. We'll be back for the reboot in five years when everyone nostalgia-bings us on streaming.

jokes.text: Brainstorming fundraising ideas: 'Or opening a zoo where the humans are in cages and the animals come to visit.'
jokes.setup: The group is brainstorming legitimate fundraising ideas
jokes.punchline: Abed contributes a fully-formed alternative reality zoo concept as a straight suggestion
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist Abed moment. The specificity of 'animals come to visit' (rather than just 'animals are free') shows genuine comedic thought — it inverts the zoo logic completely rather than just reversing it. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You should become a teacher.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Teaching? That's lame. I'm not going to be a teacher.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're homeless.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well... I'd rather be homeless than lame.

jokes.text: 'He's the one making bad bridges. That's like me blaming owls for how much I suck at analogies.'
jokes.setup: The group discusses the bridge-collapse engineer suing Greendale
jokes.punchline: Troy defends Greendale while accidentally constructing a terrible analogy about owls and analogies — the analogy itself proves the point he's trying to make
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and a strong candidate for one of the best Troy jokes in the series. The structure is self-referentially perfect: Troy uses a terrible analogy to explain why he's bad at analogies. The specific choice of 'owls' as the irrelevant scapegoat is exactly the right level of absurdist specificity. This joke only works from Troy — he's genuinely trying to be insightful. Highly quotable, structurally exceptional, could stand alongside the calibration anchors at 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Zach Braff was barely in that season. That's not cool, man. Zach Braff is a treasure.

jokes.text: Annie: 'It didn't. I love hospital administration.' Jeff: 'Is that your job?' Annie: 'Well, not yet. But I administer things to hospitals, like these. Pen?'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks how Greendale damaged Annie; she insists she loves her career
jokes.punchline: Her 'career' is revealed to be a pharmaceutical rep handing out pens — the gap between 'hospital administration' and 'giving away branded pens' is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good deflation joke. 'I administer things to hospitals, like these. Pen?' is a well-timed reveal. The disconnect between Annie's self-perception and reality is consistent with her character's earnest overreach.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Dean, did you destroy that evidence?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What? No! I would never— Look, Jeff, Greendale is a wonderful institution, and sometimes wonderful institutions have to do things that aren't exactly... wonderful. But we do them for the greater good!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: That's literally admitting you destroyed it.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm not admitting anything! I'm just saying that IF someone had destroyed evidence, it would be because our accreditation depends on maintaining certain... narratives!

jokes.text: 'They invented fibromyalgia and the cure for fibromyalgia.'
jokes.setup: Annie is praising her employer Futurza as 'a rising star in pharmaceuticals'
jokes.punchline: The company's achievement is inventing a disease and its cure simultaneously — a sharp critique of pharmaceutical industry practices delivered as a proud boast
jokes.explanation: Excellent one-liner. The concept of a pharmaceutical company inventing a disease AND its cure is a pointed satirical observation delivered with maximum economy. Annie presents it as a credential, which makes the dark subtext funnier. The choice of fibromyalgia specifically — a real condition whose validity is disputed — adds an extra layer. High quotability and genuine wit.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I was just trying to help the students... to foster an environment of learning and growth...

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Wait. No. I was doing this because it makes me look good. Because it makes ME feel important.

jokes.text: 'You push drugs now? That's ironic.' / 'I push pens, Britta.' / 'Speaking of irony, how's the therapy market? Depressed?'
jokes.setup: Britta calls out Annie for working for a pharmaceutical company given Annie's past Adderall addiction
jokes.punchline: Annie's flat 'I push pens, Britta' deflects; Britta's instant riposte 'how's the therapy market? Depressed?' — a double pun on economic depression and psychological depression
jokes.explanation: 'Depressed?' as a double-meaning punchline is sharp and efficiently constructed. The setup (Annie's ironic job) and counter-attack (Britta's failed therapy career) happen in rapid succession. Good economy and character-specific wit — these two characters sparring is well-established.

dialogue.line: Alan explaining his personal troubles. Reveals he was cheating with sisters, making it worse

jokes.text: Britta: 'I'm doing hands-on research about the psychology of alcoholism.' Jeff: 'You're a bartender, aren't you?' Britta: 'Which is basically like a modern-day therapist.'
jokes.setup: Britta claims to be on 'sabbatical' doing research
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately sees through it; Britta's rationalization ('basically like a modern-day therapist') is both defensive and kind of true, which makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Solid Britta beat. Her elaborate reframe of 'bartender' as 'psychological researcher' is consistent with her character's self-deception. Jeff's instant deflation is well-timed. Mid-tier but competent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm switching sides. I'm going to represent the other guy now.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And I'm taking all my clients with me.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff, you can't just abandon your principles like that.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Watch me. Because I'm Jeff Winger, and I'm gonna make you a believer.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Somebody tells me about a murder, I can't tell anyone.' Jeff: 'You're even bad at bartending.'
jokes.setup: Britta is defending bartending as like therapy, citing confidentiality
jokes.punchline: She accidentally describes being complicit in covering up a murder as a job perk; Jeff notes she's even failing at the new, lower bar
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke that works on both levels. Britta's murder-confidentiality reasoning is a good dark non-sequitur that she doesn't notice; Jeff's 'you're even bad at bartending' is the efficient knife-twist. Good character integration on both sides.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We could do a performance art piece about the commodification of baked goods in late-stage capitalism. We charge admission, people experience the existential dread of consumerism, and we donate the proceeds to fair-trade artisanal cooperatives.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Abed's working on the next billion-dollar social media app. And when it takes off, all I gotta do is sue him.' / 'It's foolproof.'
jokes.setup: The group shares what they've been up to post-Greendale
jokes.punchline: Troy's career plan is entirely predicated on eventually suing his best friend — presented with complete earnestness as a valid strategy
jokes.explanation: Good Troy joke. The logic is consistent with his character — absolute trust in Abed, expressed as a legal strategy. 'It's foolproof' delivered deadpan is the right punctuation. The joke also characterizes their relationship affectionately.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's like... okay, imagine blame is a hot potato, right? And everyone's passing it around, but nobody wants to hold it because it burns, so they keep throwing it—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, that's just a potato.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Exactly! See, I'm great at analogies.

jokes.text: Jeff/Abed argue about the commercial phone number: 'I didn't like the number. 555?' / 'The number of my business.' / 'Sounds fake.' / 'Every number starts with 555. Are there only 10,000 numbers?'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Abed are bickering about creative decisions on the commercial
jokes.punchline: Abed's objection to the 555 number on meta-fictional grounds ('sounds fake') and Jeff's baffled literal defense — a clash between someone who lives in narrative logic and someone who doesn't
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-comedy. Abed's rejection of 555 because 'it sounds fake' is Abed being meta-aware of TV conventions in a situation where it's genuinely absurd — it IS Jeff's real number. Jeff's 'Are there only 10,000 numbers?' is a genuinely funny response to the absurdity. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I love my career in hospital administration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Really? What exactly do you do?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I just push pens for a pharmaceutical company.

jokes.text: 'Sell him a pill that will help him give up on his dreams.' / 'Relaxabrex doesn't make you give up on your dreams. That's a side effect.'
jokes.setup: Troy is dismissive of Jeff's professional ambitions; Annie defends her pharmaceutical product
jokes.punchline: Annie's clarification that dream-killing is merely a 'side effect' of Relaxabrex is funnier than any direct joke could be — the distinction is meaningless but she insists on it
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. Annie's pedantic distinction between the drug's purpose and its side effect is a perfect satirical skewering of pharmaceutical doublespeak — and it's entirely in character for Annie to defend her employer with this technically-accurate-but-morally-hollow argument. 'That's a side effect' has the structure and delivery of a great punchline. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'At least the drugs I sell don't get slurped out of my belly button.' / 'That's only on Tummy Tuesdays! Sorry...'
jokes.setup: Annie and Britta are trading barbs about their respective drug-adjacent jobs
jokes.punchline: Annie's attack implies Britta serves shots from her belly button; Britta's horrified confirmation — 'That's only on Tummy Tuesdays!' — both confirms it and desperately contextualizes it
jokes.explanation: 'Tummy Tuesdays' is a great coinage — the specific, promotionally-branded name for a degrading bar promotion makes it funnier and sadder. Britta's reflexive capitalization ('Sorry...') adds character. High quotability on the phrase alone.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So Annie, working for a pharmaceutical company? That's quite the career move for someone with your... history.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What do you mean? I'm just doing my job.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I mean, didn't you have some issues with pills in the past? And now you're literally pushing them for a living?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That was different, Jeff. I had a problem. Now I'm helping people who actually need medication.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is... you've gone from popping pills to popping pills' career prospects?

jokes.text: Shirley quietly reveals: 'Andre left again.' [pause] 'It's not like last time. He's staying with family.' [pause] 'He took the boys, he took the dog.' [pause] 'He took the DVR.' [pause] 'Hundred and sixty-six episodes of Bones just gone.'
jokes.setup: Shirley begins what sounds like a serious personal disclosure about her husband leaving
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of losses peaks not with the boys or the dog but with the DVR full of Bones episodes — a perfect bathos about grief priorities
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent. The rhythm of the pauses — boys, dog, DVR — builds perfectly to the bathos. 'Hundred and sixty-six episodes of Bones just gone' is the right level of specific to be genuinely funny; it's not just 'episodes of TV' but a specific, almost impressively large backlog. The specificity and delivery timing make this one of the standout jokes of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm taking a sabbatical.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A sabbatical? Isn't that some kind of religious thing? Like, you're not allowed to work on Saturdays?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, Jeff. A sabbatical is a career break.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's disappointing. I was about to ask if you wanted to grab lunch on Saturday.

jokes.text: 'I cheated on him... with Shirley's Sandwiches. I threw the money into expanding. I just didn't think I could fail.'
jokes.setup: Shirley says she cheated on Andre — heavy emotional setup suggesting infidelity
jokes.punchline: The 'cheating' was with her own business — she invested money into it rather than the marriage
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection. The pause before 'with Shirley's Sandwiches' earns the reveal. The joke also works as genuine character pathos — her pride in her business was her real flaw. The punchline has emotional resonance beyond the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So what's your real job, Britta? Bartender?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Yes! And it's very serious. There's bartender-client privilege, just like lawyer-client privilege. What my customers tell me stays between us.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It absolutely is. I'm basically a therapist with a liquor license.

jokes.text: Jeff announces he needs to go to the bathroom again — his second bathroom exit in the episode
jokes.setup: Jeff is overwhelmed by what his friends have revealed and needs to escape to process his guilt
jokes.punchline: The repeated bathroom excuse, now clearly a coping mechanism / manipulation beat — the audience knows he's going to betray them
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag. The second bathroom exit earns a moderate laugh through repetition and the audience's growing awareness of its meaning. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing it's clearer what he's doing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, you're a therapist?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm studying to be one.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, that explains the confidentiality issues. You can't even keep your own secrets.

jokes.text: 'Do you guys feel weird about doing this without Magnitude?' [long pause]
jokes.setup: The group is having an emotional moment about their reunion
jokes.punchline: Troy breaks the mood by asking about Magnitude — a minor recurring character — implying he was important enough to be missed
jokes.explanation: Good comic beat. The specific choice of Magnitude — a fan-favorite one-joke character — and the pause after make this work. It's a small but deft touch: in Troy's emotional landscape, Magnitude is a core member of the group. The silence after is the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I can't direct your commercial, Jeff. You want me to use fake numbers, fake testimonials, fake before-and-after photos. That's not filmmaking—that's lying.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's advertising, Abed. That's the whole point.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. Which is why I can't do it. I have artistic integrity.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Classic Winger. I forgot what it was like to be good at being bad.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just successfully assembled his friends as plaintiffs
jokes.punchline: 'Good at being bad' — a self-aware admission that his competence is currently directed toward betraying his friends
jokes.explanation: Decent line. The self-awareness is consistent with Jeff's voice, and 'good at being bad' has a nice rhythm. Mid-tier character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know, there's always pharmaceutical solutions to life problems. I mean, why deal with your issues when you can just medicate them away?

jokes.text: Jeff's confrontation with Alan: 'You trust-funded, body-sprayed, Eli Roth DVD-owner.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is turning on Alan and needs to insult him effectively
jokes.punchline: The specific, escalating tricolon of insults — particularly 'Eli Roth DVD-owner' as the peak — creates a precisely calibrated portrait of a certain kind of empty, privileged nastiness
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. The tricolon structure ('trust-funded, body-sprayed, Eli Roth DVD-owner') escalates perfectly, and 'Eli Roth DVD-owner' as the apex insult is a stroke of specificity — it conjures a precise, recognizable type of vapid bro who enjoys torture-porn films. The word 'owner' rather than 'fan' or 'watcher' is a particularly sharp choice — it implies the DVDs are possessions of identity rather than genuine taste. Jeff uses culture as a weapon, and this is him at his most precise. Comparable to the 8+ calibration anchors.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: They're not dream-crushing pills! They're just regular pills that happen to crush dreams.

jokes.text: 'You're an amateur monster and you stomped on the grave of a real monster who was willing to stay buried because real monsters have shame...' [stops himself] 'You're not worth the monologue. Give me your tie.'
jokes.setup: Jeff begins one of his signature climactic speeches, turning the tables on Alan
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his own monologue to decide Alan isn't worth a full Winger speech — 'Give me your tie' — which is both a character statement and a meta-joke about his own speech-giving tendencies
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. The Winger monologue is a beloved Community convention; having Jeff interrupt his own mid-flow to decide the villain isn't worth it subverts the formula perfectly while BEING the formula. 'You're not worth the monologue' is a devastating cut-off that works as insult and self-awareness simultaneously. 'Give me your tie' as a non-sequitur next action is the perfect anti-climactic punctuation. Exceptional character integration — this only works because of the show's established relationship with Jeff's speeches.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: At least I don't have to do anything degrading.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Are you kidding? I have to clean the bathrooms!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Exactly.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I LOVE cleaning the bathrooms. It's the best job in the world!

jokes.text: Jeff hits Alan with the tie twice, narrating each hit: 'That's for making me go to this school.' / 'That's for making the last four years happen.' / 'And now I get to make them un-happen for me and the only people I care about.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is physically confronting Alan with the tie he just demanded
jokes.punchline: The narrated hits are mock-heroic — the speech he denied himself comes out in abbreviated tie-slap form, and the third 'hit' is just a threat, deflating the action-hero cadence
jokes.explanation: Decent physical-comedy beat that extends the joke from #50. The narrated hits are funnier than the hits themselves. The structure has some wit but leans on the previous joke's success.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: He took the TV, the dog, the cat, the kids...

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: And all my recorded episodes of The Bachelor.

jokes.text: Characters' confessions escalate: 'I failed my husband, I failed my kids. I've failed Bones.' / 'I'm helping to hook a whole new batch of little Annies on Adderall.' / 'I've spent so much time with computers your tears are 1s and 0s to me.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has asked the group to reflect on how Greendale damaged them; they're confessing failures
jokes.punchline: Three escalating self-indictments, each with a specifically funny formulation — especially Shirley's 'I've failed Bones' (the TV show) and Abed's dehumanization of tears into binary code
jokes.explanation: Strong escalating confessions sequence. 'I've failed Bones' callbacks perfectly to the DVR joke and elevates it. Abed's '1s and 0s' is exactly the right kind of Abed-specific self-revelation. These three lines do a lot of character work efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I know I haven't been the best wife. I've been so focused on my business, I haven't given Andre the attention he deserves.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: Shirley, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I've been unfaithful, Andre. I've been seeing someone else. We've been together for months now, and it's gotten very serious.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I invested fifty thousand dollars in a yogurt franchise.

jokes.text: 'I'm helping to hook a whole new batch of little Annies on Adderall.'
jokes.setup: Annie is confessing her failures; she sells pharmaceuticals
jokes.punchline: She references her own backstory (she was addicted to Adderall) and reveals she is now perpetuating the cycle she survived
jokes.explanation: A devastating character callback. Only works for long-term viewers who know Annie's history with Adderall addiction. The irony is pitch-black: she was destroyed by Adderall, lost her academic career, went to Greendale — and now she's literally selling the drug to new students. The phrase 'little Annies' is particularly sharp — she identifies with the victims. Strong character integration, earned dark humor.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I know what this looks like, but if you just listen to what I'm saying...

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: The Winger Speech. I've seen this move a hundred times. You lean against something, you gesture with your hands, you make it all sound sincere...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Isn't it? Because right now you're about to tilt your head and tell me why rules don't apply to you.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Yeah, you were a real Hallmark card before.' Troy: 'I'm much sadder than the rest of you.' [pause] 'I will figure out why later.'
jokes.setup: Abed's cold emotional dehumanization of his friends prompts Jeff's sarcasm; Troy then makes his own claim
jokes.punchline: Troy's assertion of superior sadness with zero supporting evidence, followed by deferring the proof to a later date — confident and utterly unexamined
jokes.explanation: 'I will figure out why later' is an exceptional Troy line. His absolute confidence in his own sadness combined with his complete lack of introspective evidence is perfectly Troy — big feelings, zero processing. The deferred self-examination is both funny and strangely poignant. High quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what, Alan? You're not just a bad person. You're a bad person in a very specific way. You have the confidence of someone attractive combined with the intelligence of someone who thinks a reversible belt is a personality trait. You're the kind of guy who would high-five himself in the mirror if you could figure out how mirrors work. And your handwriting looks like a seizure had a baby with a parking ticket.

jokes.text: Chang appears and reveals: 'I dropped the amnesia thing, copped to my crimes and went to jail. Now I'm on work release.' / 'Working as what?' / 'Math teacher.'
jokes.setup: Chang mysteriously appears; the group reacts to seeing 'Kevin'
jokes.punchline: His post-jail re-employment is as a math teacher at the same school — reinstated to a teaching position after his entire criminal arc
jokes.explanation: Good institutional-absurdity joke. Chang being rehired as a math teacher after his entire criminal saga is exactly the kind of Greendale incompetence the episode is about. 'Math teacher' as the flat punchline is correctly delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to say something, and I want you all to really listen, because this is important and—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, no. I'm doing it again. I'm doing that thing where I build to some dramatic moment and everyone just stares at me like I'm about to say something profound, and honestly, it's getting old.

jokes.text: Chang explains his ankle monitor situation: he's on work release from house arrest but doesn't have a home, so he's tethered to a 30-yard cord attached to this building. 'I can only travel—' / 'You do the math.' / 'You said you teach math.' / 'Exactly. I teach it, you do it.'
jokes.setup: Chang explains his complicated monitoring situation and invites Jeff to calculate his range
jokes.punchline: 'You do the math' / 'You said you teach math' / 'Exactly. I teach it, you do it.' — a perfect deadpan teacher-logic response
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy. The three-line exchange is structurally immaculate — setup, challenge, and comeback. 'I teach it, you do it' is a perfect teacher-logic deflection that is simultaneously arrogant and defensible. The structure builds to the punchline efficiently, and the line is highly quotable. Chang at his most effective.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I don't have any problems. I'm just a collection of pop culture references and quirks.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Chang was faking his Changnesia?' / Abed: 'Seriously rehired a teacher they fired for trying to burn down the school.' / [someone]: 'After being rehired as a guard after being fired for impersonating a teacher.' / Abed: 'That's insane, and I'm Abed.'
jokes.setup: The group processes Chang's history of crimes and reemployments
jokes.punchline: Abed's 'That's insane, and I'm Abed' — a character who exists on the edge of institutional sanity rating something as beyond his threshold
jokes.explanation: 'That's insane, and I'm Abed' is a great punchline because Abed as the character-who-processes-everything-through-narrativized-distance serving as the sanity barometer is perfect. His acknowledgment of his own institutional weirdness as a calibration point is exactly the kind of meta-character-integration Community does best. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've become less emotional due to all this computer work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, you were never emotional to begin with.

jokes.text: Alan: 'I may be evil, but your friend here is so much more dangerous. Tell them how it took you 30 minutes to make them think they wanted to sue their own school.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just dramatically turned on Alan; Alan retaliates by exposing Jeff's manipulation
jokes.punchline: '30 minutes' — the specificity of the timeframe makes the manipulation sound almost more insulting than if it had taken longer
jokes.explanation: Decent beat. '30 minutes' is the right comedic precision — it's both fast enough to be insulting to the friends and specific enough to be funny rather than vague. The beat lands as both a plot beat and a comedic one.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm going to need you all to understand that I'm experiencing genuine sadness right now, which is statistically significant because my emotional baseline is typically 40% detached irony.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've been cataloging my grief in a spreadsheet using the Kübler-Ross model as a framework, and I'm currently oscillating between anger and bargaining, which I've color-coded for clarity.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Also, I'm sad in a way that's narratively satisfying, which means I should probably have a montage set to an indie folk song.

jokes.text: Alan: 'Anyway, I'll leave you to pick up these pieces. I'm gonna go score some blow. My dealer's a gym teacher here.'
jokes.setup: Alan makes his exit after exposing Jeff
jokes.punchline: He casually announces his next errand is buying cocaine from a Greendale gym teacher — delivered as a final, throwaway Greendale-is-broken data point
jokes.explanation: Good throwaway joke. 'My dealer's a gym teacher here' as an exit line perfectly encapsulates Greendale's dysfunction — it's both a character moment for Alan and another institutional indictment. The casualness of the delivery is correct.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang? What are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about. My name is Kevin.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Kevin? Come on, we all know you're Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I have no memory of being Chang. I only remember being Kevin.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Troy, your entire identity has been consumed by your relationship with another man.' Troy: 'You found my Clive Owen Tumblr.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is criticizing Troy for losing himself in his friendship with Abed
jokes.punchline: Troy's instant assumption that Jeff found his Clive Owen Tumblr — the existence of which is funnier than any explanation, and completely recontextualizes 'relationship with another man'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quotable jokes. The structure is flawless: Jeff's vague reference to 'relationship with another man' could mean Abed, but Troy's panic-reveal of a secret Clive Owen Tumblr is both unexpected and entirely consistent with his character. The specificity of Clive Owen (a suave British actor, slightly unexpected as an object of Troy's devotion) makes it funnier than a generic celebrity. The word 'Tumblr' perfectly dates and contextualizes the obsession. Exceptional economy — zero wasted words.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, you were a math teacher. Can you help us with this equation?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No. I don't do math anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You don't... do math? You taught math.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That was a different Chang. A Chang who had hope. A Chang who believed in numbers.

jokes.text: Jeff references 'the gas leak year' — a coded reference to the show's troubled Season 4
jokes.setup: Annie tries to attribute the group's regression to 'that gas leak last year'
jokes.punchline: The 'gas leak year' is a Community in-joke explaining away Season 4's tonal inconsistencies — acknowledged and dismissed by Jeff: 'Oh, don't blame it all on the gas leak year'
jokes.explanation: Classic Community meta-joke. 'The gas leak year' as an in-universe explanation for the show's fourth season (which was made without Dan Harmon) is one of the most audacious self-referential meta-jokes in the show's history. The casualness of its use here — as if it's just a known fact — makes it land harder. Rewatch bonus is high because fans get increasingly more from it.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Chang's been employed here as a security guard, lunch lady, and dean. He's basically Greendale's version of a Swiss Army knife, except one of the blades is insanity.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I use myself as the baseline for normal behavior, so by that metric, Chang's doing fine.

jokes.text: 'But you're our hero.' / 'I mean, in the commercial...' / Jeff: 'The commercial was a lie.' / [group]: 'You staged a robot fight?' / Jeff: 'Yeah. In real life, the robot wins.'
jokes.setup: Jeff's heroic commercial is cited as evidence of his heroism
jokes.punchline: 'In real life, the robot wins' — a callback to the commercial's villain ('I am the system') with an admission that Jeff actually loses to the system in real life
jokes.explanation: 'In real life, the robot wins' is a great line — it callbacks the opening while delivering a thematically resonant punchline about Jeff's real limitations. The specificity ('the robot,' not 'I lose') is nicely defeatist. Strong economy and structural callback.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The school's problems are like a diseased organ that needs to be removed before it spreads to the rest of the body. Except the body is education and the organ is... well, Greendale itself.

jokes.text: Troy says: 'If Jeff didn't change, then Jeff is right.' — delivered with quiet certainty
jokes.setup: The group is debating whether to sue Greendale
jokes.punchline: Troy's logical syllogism sounds profound but on examination it's circular and somewhat nonsensical — yet everyone accepts it as the decisive argument
jokes.explanation: Troy's quasi-logical declarations are a character staple. This one almost makes sense on second reading which makes it funnier — it's not entirely wrong, just slightly off-axis.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Yeah, I gotta go. By the way, I've been buying cocaine from Professor Hickey for three years now.

jokes.text: Pierce appears as a hologram: 'Jesus.' / 'Looks as if you've lost your way.' / 'Pierce?' / Pierce explains the hologram was 'donated in compliance with a court order I'm not allowed to discuss. Let's just say some women can't take a compliment.'
jokes.setup: Jeff encounters what appears to be Pierce's ghost/hologram on the quad
jokes.punchline: Pierce's hologram exists because of a sexual harassment court order — 'some women can't take a compliment' — revealing that even his posthumous monument is rooted in his worst qualities
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce exit moment. 'The Pierce Hawthorne Museum of Gender Sensitivity and Sexual Potency' is a great name, and 'donated in compliance with a court order' as the reason for a museum is perfectly absurd. 'Some women can't take a compliment' as Pierce's characteristically oblivious spin on sexual harassment is perfectly in character — this is exactly how Pierce would explain it. Strong character integration for a character who is gone.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, you've really come into your own this year. You know, when you first got here, you were just this crazy, impulsive girl. But now? Now you're a crazy, impulsive woman.

jokes.text: Pierce hologram: 'Did I sound gay at the end? Do you wanna do another take?'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just delivered a surprisingly warm, genuine speech about Greendale
jokes.punchline: He immediately shatters the sincerity by worrying that the earnestness made him 'sound gay' — both a Pierce character moment and a meta-break of the fourth wall
jokes.explanation: 'Do you wanna do another take?' breaks the fourth wall in a specifically Pierce way — his sincere speech was apparently filmed and he's now in the editing process. The meta-awareness that he's a hologram performing a recorded message is funny, and his immediate reversion to Pierce-isms after a brief moment of genuine warmth is both funny and sad. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, did you just call me an airhead?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh! Thank you! I thought you were going to say something mean.

jokes.text: Dean: 'It's my whole ideantity.' [immediately catches himself] 'I mean... See what I did there? That's proof.'
jokes.setup: Dean is defending his identity as being tied to his deanship
jokes.punchline: He accidentally says 'ideantity' (identity + dean), then immediately recognizes it and treats it as evidence of his psychological merger with the role
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dean Pelton moment. 'Ideantity' is a great accidental portmanteau, and his immediate recognition and use of it as self-diagnosis ('See what I did there? That's proof') is pitch-perfect character comedy. Only Dean Pelton has this relationship to his job title. The wordplay is organic rather than forced.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're way too dependent on Abed. You need to develop your own identity, your own interests.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is this about the blog?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What blog?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My celebrity crush blog. Abed said he wouldn't tell anyone.

jokes.text: Dean: 'But you could stay here and help me save the school.' Jeff: 'For how much money?' Dean: 'I can't offer you any money.' Jeff: 'You just described slavery.'
jokes.setup: Dean offers Jeff a job saving the school
jokes.punchline: 'You just described slavery' — Jeff's instant, hyperbolic legal response to being asked to work for free
jokes.explanation: Good quick joke. 'You just described slavery' as an instant, deadpan escalation of 'unpaid work' is a solid Jeff line — legally technical, hyperbolic, delivered flatly. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We can blame it on the gas leak year.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's what the writers do.

jokes.text: Dean: 'There's nothing in the budget for school-saver, but I could hire you as...' Jeff: 'Screw you, Abed.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is about to offer Jeff the job title 'Professor Winger' — which Abed has presumably already revealed to Jeff off-screen
jokes.punchline: Jeff knows exactly what's coming (teacher, as Abed predicted) and directs his anger not at the Dean but at Abed, for being right
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The Dean hasn't even said 'teacher' yet, but Jeff knows — and his anger is directed at Abed, not the person hiring him. 'Screw you, Abed' is an economically perfect line that closes the Scrubs/repilot meta-arc while being genuinely funny. The implication is that Abed's narrative prediction is so accurate that Jeff is furious at the author, not the circumstance.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The commercial was fake. I made it up.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you LIED? Jeff, that's... hold on. You're telling me you paid someone to be in a fake commercial?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: And you faked all those testimonials?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But... did you at least use real yogurt?

jokes.text: Britta sitting alone: 'I'd be depressed if these samples from work weren't giving me a new outlook on life.' [cheerful, possibly medicated] 'If you're interested in learning more, ask your doctor if Joyvatrex is right for you.'
jokes.setup: Britta is alone and should be processing the emotional events of the episode
jokes.punchline: She's apparently sampling her own pharmaceutical products and delivers an ad-read for 'Joyvatrex' — a fake drug whose name implies forced joy
jokes.explanation: Good bit. 'Joyvatrex' is a good fake drug name. The ad-read delivery is consistent with Annie's pharma-rep world bleeding into Britta's. The meta-frame of a drug commercial inserted into a character moment is appropriately dark. Mid-tier but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I don't know what you expect. Robots are just going to get smarter and smarter until they realize they don't need us. Then it's game over for humanity.

jokes.text: Pierce hologram pops up: 'Oh, honey.' Jeff: 'If we sue Greendale, can I be a surprise witness?' [Pierce] / 'Wait. Don't tell me.' / Jeff/group: 'Stop.'
jokes.setup: Pierce's hologram reappears unexpectedly
jokes.punchline: Pierce's eagerness to be a 'surprise witness' in a lawsuit — and his 'Wait. Don't tell me' suggesting he wants to guess the case details — is exactly the kind of unhelpful enthusiasm Pierce always brought
jokes.explanation: Decent Pierce callback. The eagerness to participate in something he doesn't understand is very Pierce. Mid-tier execution — the first hologram appearance was funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I want to burn the study table.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's like petty theft — I'm only doing it because I'm better than everyone else, so normal rules don't apply to me.

jokes.text: Annie: 'We shouldn't sue the school.' / 'Oh, come on!' / 'Are you trying to give us emotional whiplash?'
jokes.setup: The group has just been convinced to sue Greendale; Annie reverses course
jokes.punchline: 'Are you trying to give us emotional whiplash?' — the group's exasperated meta-awareness of how many times their position has changed in this episode
jokes.explanation: 'Emotional whiplash' is a funny, accurate description of the episode's structure — the group has been emotionally pivoted at least three times. Mid-tier meta joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I got a court order about gender sensitivity, but that's just because I said one little thing about a woman's appearance.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: How was I supposed to know that commenting on her assets was sexual harassment? I was just being friendly!

jokes.text: Jeff: 'You got a job teaching here.' Jeff: 'I don't wanna talk about it.'
jokes.setup: The group is sharing what they're going to do next; they note Jeff is teaching
jokes.punchline: Jeff's flat 'I don't wanna talk about it' — refusing to acknowledge the full Abed-was-right situation
jokes.explanation: Functional running-gag closer. Jeff's refusal to acknowledge the irony is in character. The joke is mild but correctly deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce Hologram
dialogue.line: Look, Greendale may be a crappy place, but it's OUR crappy place. And I may be a terrible person, but at least I'm terrible here.

jokes.text: Britta: 'I'm gonna get a four-year psych degree, then a master's, and become a real psychologist.' / Jeff: 'Or you could find another major.' / 'Psychology.' / 'How about English?' / 'Psychology.' / 'All right, what's important is no matter what, we'll be trying to talk Britta into doing something different together.'
jokes.setup: Britta announces her plan to pursue psychology
jokes.punchline: Jeff's attempts to redirect her into anything else are batted down identically, until he frames his own defeat as a group bonding experience
jokes.explanation: Good Britta/Jeff dynamic joke. 'We'll be trying to talk Britta into doing something different together' is a great closing line — it reframes Britta's stubbornness as a group activity rather than a loss. Strong character integration on both sides.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I want you all to know that I love you guys, and I'm really going to miss—wait, is this still recording? Because I don't want people to think I'm gay.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Burn, hopelessness.' [lights the table on fire] — only to realize the room is immediately on fire
jokes.setup: Jeff dramatically announces he'll burn the study room table as a symbolic act
jokes.punchline: The fire immediately gets out of control, turning the gesture into a disaster
jokes.explanation: 'Burn, hopelessness' as an incantation before accidentally starting a fire is a decent physical comedy beat. The gap between Jeff's intended symbolism and the actual result is funny but fairly predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I can't stop being Dean. It's not just a job, it's a... Dean-tiny!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Did you catch that? Dean-tiny. Destiny. I'll be here all week.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton, watching the fire: 'Little victories count for a lot around here.'
jokes.setup: The room is on fire; this is objectively a disaster
jokes.punchline: The Dean frames a burning room as a 'little victory' — total institutional dysfunction delivered with sincere administrative positivity
jokes.explanation: Good Dean Pelton line. The gap between 'room on fire' and 'little victories' is wide enough to generate genuine laughter. His administrative optimism in the face of objective failure is a defining character trait deployed perfectly here.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So let me get this straight. You want me to work for you, but you're not going to pay me.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, it's more of an opportunity for experience and—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's called slavery, Dean. You're describing slavery.

jokes.text: Voice-over: 'He does a voice-over wrap-up at the end of every episode.' / 'Cool.' / 'Because around here, they never last very long.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is doing an end-of-episode philosophical voice-over
jokes.punchline: Abed interrupts the voice-over to point out that Jeff does a voice-over wrap-up at the end of every episode — the fourth wall broken mid-monologue
jokes.explanation: Good meta-moment. Abed interrupting Jeff's voice-over to identify the convention it represents is very on-brand, and Jeff's slightly defensive 'Cool.' before continuing is well-deployed. The 'they never last very long' line is a good meta-coda about the show's renewal anxiety.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is all your fault, Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: How is this my fault?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You knew this would happen. You manipulated me into taking this job.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I didn't manipulate you. I just predicted what you would do.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's the same thing!

jokes.text: Post-credits: Dean Pelton directing Jeff's new teacher-intro video. Jeff says 'I wanna kill myself.' Dean: 'Use that.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is filming what appears to be an institutional teacher introduction video and is frustrated
jokes.punchline: 'Use that' — Dean Pelton enthusiastically incorporating Jeff's suicidal despair into the promotional material for a community college
jokes.explanation: Strong closing joke. 'Use that' is a perfectly economical punchline — the Dean's oblivious enthusiasm for Jeff's despair captures both characters perfectly and is a good dark note to end on. The callback to Jeff's commercial from the opening creates a bookend structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And that's the lesson we learned today about friendship and—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're doing the thing where the main character gives the moral lesson at the end of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know what I'm doing.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Do you though? Because you're literally standing in a spotlight that wasn't here five seconds ago.

jokes.text: Post-credits commercial parody: 'Are you a good person? Yes, unlike you.' / 'I can guarantee, the Winger beaten you. Not anymore.'
jokes.setup: The episode ends with another version of Jeff's lawyer commercial
jokes.punchline: The new commercial is garbled and self-contradictory — 'the Winger beaten you. Not anymore.' — suggesting this take is even worse than the original
jokes.explanation: Decent bookend callback. The new commercial being worse/more garbled than the original is a consistent joke about Jeff's diminished state. Mid-tier but serves the structural purpose of closing the episode's commercial arc.

jokes.text: Post-credits: Jeff's new commercial: 'Are you a good person? Yes, unlike you. I can guarantee, the Winger beaten you. Not anymore.'
jokes.setup: Callback to the opening commercial
jokes.punchline: Jeff's new commercial is worse — the script is mangled, the delivery is desperate, and the tagline makes no sense
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural bookend. The opening commercial was bad; the closing one is worse — 'the Winger beaten you' doesn't even make grammatical sense. The joke suggests that even with a fresh start, Jeff's commercial still communicates exhaustion and incoherence. Good callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Chang farts and laughs at his own fart

tmdb_overview: With his law practice doomed, Jeff returns to Greendale to start a class action suit against the school, but a hologram of Pierce has him reconsider.
insight: Season 5 reboot lands 75 jokes in 24 minutes—character-driven chaos sustains the show's return.
